justification: Switches four already-written runtime postconditions from no-ops to live on the served flood path, adds a fifth that was never there, and makes the tests guarding them able to fail. Changes runtime behaviour in production (a violated contract raises instead of returning a bad value) but adds no feature, no DB access and no user-facing text. Standard rather than critical because the contracts assert properties the code already satisfies — verified by running the whole suite with them enforcing.

falsifiable_check.command: pip install icontract && python -m pytest tests/ -q --tb=short ; python -m pytest tests/test_flood_truth.py -q -k icontract ; python scripts/check_dependency_skips.py
falsifiable_check.passes_when: The whole suite runs with contracts ENFORCING and reports 0 failures (3704 passed), all five icontract tests pass rather than skip, and the skip ratchet matches its lowered baseline of 18.
falsifiable_check.fails_when: Any icontract.ViolationError during the suite — that would mean a contract is stricter than the code it guards, and turning it on would convert working flood reports into 500s. That is the real risk of this change and the reason the check is 'run everything with them on' rather than 'run the five contract tests'. The ratchet fails if the baseline is not lowered to lock the recovered coverage in.
falsifiable_check.demonstrated_failing: Four states reproduced. (1) Before: all five tests SKIP in every environment — icontract was declared only in scripts/requirements-maintenance.txt, so the _FakeIcontract no-ops ran in production, CI and local alike. (2) Installing icontract on the pre-change tree makes 4 of 5 pass and 1 still skip, which is how _compute_flood_signal was found to have no decorator at all — confirmed absent in both commits that ever touched it (9977134d, e35a7641). (3) After the change, deleting the new decorator makes the test FAIL with 'icontract IS installed, so the @icontract.ensure decorator has been removed or was never added' — previously the identical state produced a silent skip. (4) The skip census drops 23 to 18 and the ratchet refuses to pass until the baseline is lowered.
falsifiable_check.mutation_evidence: Remove the @icontract.ensure on _compute_flood_signal -> test_icontract_signal_contract_active fails (verified, then restored). Revert _check_postcondition to skipping on a missing __postconditions__ -> decorator removal becomes invisible again. Drop icontract from services/requirements.txt -> the container installs without it and every contract silently reverts to a no-op, the state this change ends. Leave the baseline at 23 -> the ratchet fails, so the recovery cannot be quietly undone later.
falsifiable_check.self_comparison_note: Not a self-comparison: the contracts are asserted by installing the real library and observing __postconditions__ on the actual function objects, and the safety evidence is the entire suite executing with those contracts enforcing rather than a re-run of the same code path against itself.

pre_impl.existing_data: No DB access. Investigated 2026-08-06 with no changes made: icontract appears in scripts/requirements-maintenance.txt only. Dockerfile.python:26-27 copies and installs services/requirements.txt, which did not list it, so the deployed container has always run the _FakeIcontract fallback. requirements.txt and requirements-test.txt did not list it either. Four @icontract.ensure decorators exist in services/flood_truth.py; a fifth function named by the tests had none.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: The test helper's own docstring claimed 'In CI (GitHub Actions), icontract is installed cleanly and these tests run.' That was false, and it is why the skip went unexamined. Also corrected: this looked at first like five inert contracts, but it is four inert contracts plus one that never existed — a different defect that the shared skip concealed. Mitigating fact found during the investigation and worth stating plainly: Hypothesis DOES run (it is in requirements-test.txt) and its four property tests already assert the signal enum, the gap-reason shape and the source-count bounds, so this was a missing runtime guard on top of live test-time coverage, not an unguarded surface.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: Nothing new is authored. The four contracts were already written and correct; this declares the library where it is actually installed so they execute. The fifth decorator reuses _VALID_FLOOD_SIGNALS, the module constant already shared by the _normalise_outputs contract and the Hypothesis enum test, so the three cannot drift apart.

functions.name: _compute_flood_signal
functions.input: the internal outputs dict assembled from the nine flood sources
functions.output: one of none/low/moderate/elevated/unavailable, now guarded by a postcondition it never had
functions.if_none: returns 'unavailable' explicitly when the EPI query failed — that is a valid enum member, not an absence

functions.name: _compute_confidence
functions.input: the same internal outputs dict, after the signal is computed
functions.output: low/medium/high, with its contract now live rather than a no-op
functions.if_none: cannot return None — the branches are exhaustive and end at 'low'

functions.name: _check_postcondition
functions.input: a function object and its name, from each of the five contract tests
functions.output: passes when a postcondition is attached, FAILS when icontract is present and it is not, skips only when the library is genuinely absent
functions.if_none: a missing library is the one case that still skips, and scripts/check_dependency_skips.py counts that so it cannot hide

values.if_missing: an unrecognised string now raises at the boundary instead of reaching the badge renderer, where it showed as blank
raises rather than rendering a broken badge on the report and PDF
an out-of-range count would corrupt the refuse-to-serve threshold; it now raises instead

queries.purpose: none — this change performs no database access at all
queries.if_wrong: n/a: the contracts are pure-function postconditions evaluated on values already in memory, so there is no query to get wrong

break_it.scenario: a contract is stricter than the code it guards, so a real flood report starts raising
break_it.what_happens: working reports become 500s — the one way this change could make things worse rather than better
break_it.how: the entire suite was run with contracts ENFORCING: 3704 passed, zero ViolationError, including the four Hypothesis property tests that drive randomised inputs through the newly decorated function. The contracts assert properties the code already satisfies.
break_it.repro: pip install icontract && python -m pytest tests/ -q

break_it.scenario: someone deletes a decorator later, or adds a return branch with a string not in the enum
break_it.what_happens: before this change the guarding test skipped silently, so removal was undetectable — the mutant each test claims to kill was the one mutant it could not see
break_it.how: with icontract installed a missing postcondition is now an assertion failure naming the function; only a genuinely absent library skips
break_it.repro: delete the @icontract.ensure above _compute_flood_signal and run pytest -k icontract_signal — fails (verified, then restored)

break_it.scenario: icontract is dropped from services/requirements.txt in a future dependency tidy-up
break_it.what_happens: the container silently reverts to _FakeIcontract and all five contracts become no-ops again, with nothing red
break_it.how: the five tests then skip, and the dependency-skip ratchet sees icontract reappear as a NEW dependency against a baseline that no longer lists it, so the build fails
break_it.repro: uninstall icontract and run python scripts/check_dependency_skips.py — exits 1

break_it.scenario: a violation fires in production and the caller sees a 500 instead of a report
break_it.what_happens: an error rather than a report — worse for that one request than a slightly wrong badge would have been
break_it.how: accepted deliberately, and it is the point of the change: a wrong flood signal on a compliance report is the liability, a 500 is an inconvenience, and the project's own rule already ranks silent wrong data as the worse outcome. Not caught and downgraded to a soft response, because swallowing a violation would recreate exactly the silent-bad-value behaviour being removed.
break_it.repro: n/a — no input in the suite triggers a violation; this is the accepted consequence if one ever does

break_it.scenario: the recovered coverage is quietly lost again by leaving the baseline loose at 23
break_it.what_happens: skips drift back up and nothing objects, exactly as they did for the whole life of these tests
break_it.how: the baseline is lowered to 18 in this same commit, and the ratchet matches exactly in both directions

post_merge.db_reset: No. No migration and no DB access.
post_merge.other_repo: No. The Railway container rebuilds from Dockerfile.python and picks up services/requirements.txt on deploy.
post_merge.manual_verify: 1) After deploy, generate one flood report and confirm it still renders — that is the live proof no contract misfires on real data. 2) Confirm CI shows the dependency-skip census at 18 rather than 23. 3) Check the build log for the icontract wheel, or run python -c 'import icontract' in the deployed container, to confirm the contracts are actually live rather than silently falling back.
